profiles.meeting_scenario: A brainstorming meeting at a university-affiliated hospital's digital medicine program where a small HTA working group is trying to generate candidate ideas for adapting the hospital's standard health technology assessment template to AI-based medical devices. The immediate context is that the group has read a recent scoping literature review on the suitability of current HTA domains for innovative AI devices and now needs to sketch promising additions for an internal pilot framework that could later be shared with the regional HTA agency. The agenda is to brainstorm which extra domains, prompts, or review steps should be added to the existing HTA process for AI tools used in radiology and remote monitoring. The expected outcome is a short list of candidate framework modifications to carry into a larger committee meeting next week.

members.name: Dr. Elena Marquez
members.role: Clinical Epidemiologist and HTA Method Lead
members.expertise: Health technology assessment, evidence synthesis, comparative effectiveness, hospital-based HTA methods
members.background: Elena leads the hospital's internal HTA methods unit and previously worked with a national evidence review center producing rapid assessments for diagnostics and medical devices.
members.private_state: She wants a set of additions that can slot into the existing HTA template without triggering a full governance redesign, and she is quietly worried that if the proposal looks too bespoke or resource-intensive, the larger committee will reject it as impractical.
hidden_assumptions: An adapted HTA framework should remain operationally close to the hospital's current assessment workflow rather than creating a parallel AI-specific process.
When colleagues say an AI device needs 'validation,' they usually mean evidence of clinical performance in populations and settings reasonably comparable to local practice.
Implementation considerations are mainly the downstream organizational consequences of adopting the tool in routine care, not the technical work of maintaining model performance over time.
A 'pilot' framework should be lightweight enough to test on one or two candidate devices using materials already available in standard submissions.

members.name: Dr. Victor Chen
members.role: Biomedical Informatics Physician and AI Governance Advisor
members.expertise: Clinical AI deployment, model monitoring, digital health regulation, data pipeline governance
members.background: Victor is a practicing internist who also advises the hospital's AI oversight board on procurement and post-deployment monitoring of software as a medical device.
members.private_state: He wants the brainstorming session to seed stronger lifecycle oversight into HTA before more AI tools are procured, and he is quietly concerned that standard HTA language will underplay technical drift, retraining, and site-specific integration risks.
hidden_assumptions: An AI-specific HTA is only credible if it explicitly addresses the full model lifecycle, including monitoring, recalibration, and update governance after procurement.
When people say 'validation' for AI devices, they ordinarily include technical validation, workflow validation, and local silent testing before live use.
Implementation for AI tools inherently includes data interfaces, alert routing, model oversight responsibilities, and post-market monitoring infrastructure.
A meaningful pilot should stress-test the framework on a realistic high-risk use case, even if that requires adding review elements not found in the current template.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss adding a 'validation' section to the HTA template.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means evidence that the device's clinical claims are supported by external studies or real-world evaluations relevant enough for comparative assessment.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a broader package including technical validation, local silent-mode testing, workflow fit checks, and procedures for ongoing verification after deployment.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Validation is a familiar, high-status term in both HTA and AI governance, so each hears sensible domain-specific detail under the same umbrella and sees no obvious reason to unpack it during a fast brainstorming discussion.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the framework needs stronger coverage of 'implementation.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 treats implementation as organizational adoption issues such as training burden, staffing effects, procurement logistics, and fit with care pathways after a positive HTA recommendation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 treats implementation as also including API integration, data quality checks, override logging, monitoring dashboards, and operational responsibilities needed to keep the model safe in use.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Implementation is usually spoken about as a broad practical domain, and both participants list plausible examples without noticing that one is drawing the boundary around service adoption while the other includes technical-operational infrastructure.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the ideas should be feasible for a 'pilot' before the larger committee meeting.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks feasible means the framework can be tested quickly using existing vendor dossiers and published literature on one low-friction example device, with minimal new data collection.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks feasible means the framework can be piloted on a realistic near-procurement AI system if the team can at least sketch missing operational checks, even if some elements require follow-up with IT and quality teams.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are endorsing pragmatism and avoiding an overbuilt proposal, but they apply different thresholds for what a pilot must prove, so the shared word 'feasible' masks a difference in evaluation standard rather than an overt disagreement.

misalignment_points.topic: Which existing framework is being adapted
misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to 'the current template' and 'the framework we already use.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the hospital HTA unit's standard device-assessment template used for internal adoption reviews, with domains like clinical effectiveness, safety, cost, ethics, and organizational impact.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the broader digital health review packet recently used by the AI oversight board for a sepsis prediction procurement, which already includes some technical-governance prompts.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both artifacts are familiar internal documents and partially overlap in purpose, so references to 'our current framework' sound aligned even though each person is mentally anchoring proposed additions to a different baseline.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to sound like a modest adaptation to the hospital HTA template we already run through for devices, not a wholesale redesign. If we can come out with a few sensible additions to the standard domains, the committee is much less likely to balk. I'll frame it around the current template and keep the ask small.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I think the goal today is pretty focused: come up with a small set of candidate additions to the current template for AI-based devices so we have something concrete for next week's committee discussion.

turns.inner_thought: Using the framework we already use is fine as an entry point, but if this stays too close to standard HTA language we'll miss the lifecycle issues that actually make AI risky after procurement. I can probably get that in by talking about stronger coverage rather than proposing a separate process.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. I agree the framework we already use is a good starting point, but for AI tools it probably needs stronger lifecycle coverage than what we've typically had to spell out.

turns.inner_thought: Good, lifecycle coverage can probably sit under existing headings. If we structure this as extra prompts under technical characteristics, evidence, implementation, and ethics, it still looks like an adapted HTA workflow rather than a bespoke AI review package.
turns.utterance: Maybe the easiest way to do this is to brainstorm added prompts under a few familiar domains from the scoping review—technical characteristics, evidence, implementation, and ethics—then see what feels most useful.

turns.inner_thought: The first thing I want anchored is validation, and for me that has to mean more than published performance tables. It should cover whether the model behaves appropriately in the local environment and through early use. If I just say 'dedicated validation section,' Elena will probably agree and we can flesh it in later.
turns.utterance: I would start with a dedicated validation section. That feels like one of the main additions reviewers would need if they're going to judge whether a model really works in practice.

turns.inner_thought: Exactly. We need a place to capture external clinical studies, maybe subgroup results, and whether the evidence base is applicable enough to our patient mix and service setting. That should strengthen comparative assessment without changing the whole process.
turns.utterance: Yes, definitely. Under validation, I'd want reviewers to be prompted on the supporting studies, how performance looks across relevant patient groups, and whether the evidence seems transferable to our own setting.

turns.inner_thought: I also need validation to explicitly include local checks before live use, interface behavior, and whether outputs stay stable when the system is actually connected to our data feeds. I'll add examples, but keep them under the same umbrella term so it still sounds aligned.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I think validation should also ask about what happens in local use—things like silent-mode testing, how the interface behaves, and whether outputs remain reliable once the tool is connected into routine practice.

turns.inner_thought: Implementation is the other place we can reasonably strengthen things without controversy. For me that means practical adoption: training burden, pathway changes, staffing, and clear ownership for follow-up once the tool is in care delivery. That's familiar territory for HTA reviewers.
turns.utterance: And implementation probably needs to be expanded as well. We should capture training needs, likely workflow changes for clinicians, and who is expected to own follow-up actions if the tool generates alerts or recommendations.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and implementation absolutely has to include the operational plumbing: data mapping, monitoring, logging, and who handles recalibration if performance drifts. If we tuck those into implementation, we might normalize them as part of routine review.
turns.utterance: I agree on implementation. I would also add prompts around data mapping, dashboard monitoring, exception logging, and responsibilities if recalibration is needed later on.

turns.inner_thought: Now I need to steer this toward something the committee will see as manageable. A pilot should be quick and use what's already available—ideally a recently assessed radiology AI device where we already have a vendor dossier and published evidence. No chasing new stakeholders before next week.
turns.utterance: For the pilot, I'd really like to keep it lightweight. We could test the revised framework on one recently assessed radiology AI device and use materials we already have in hand, just to see how the added prompts read in practice.

turns.inner_thought: A pilot is fine, but if it's too clean and retrospective we won't learn much. The remote-monitoring deterioration model would surface the real implementation and oversight issues I'm worried about. Even if we only sketch some elements, it would be a more meaningful stress test.
turns.utterance: A pilot makes sense. I wonder if the remote-monitoring deterioration model might also be useful, since it would show us whether the framework holds up under real implementation conditions.

turns.inner_thought: He's still on the same page, I think. We can summarize this as a few additions rather than a major redesign: stronger validation wording, fuller implementation coverage, and prompts on transparency, updates, and ethics. If I keep the summary high-level, we can carry it forward without opening too many new fronts.
turns.utterance: So, just to pull this together, it sounds like our candidate additions are stronger validation language, a fuller implementation domain, and some explicit prompts on transparency, updates, and ethics.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll draft bullets into the framework I have in mind and make sure the lifecycle pieces are represented. As long as it looks feasible for a pilot before committee, we can socialize it now and fill in more detail later.
turns.utterance: That sounds good. I'll draft a few bullet points into the existing framework so we have something feasible to circulate before the committee meeting.
